evidence.claim: A riverside road follows the Mystic’s east bank into Old Mystic.
evidence.quote: The road along the east bank of the Mystic River, connecting the villages of Mystic and Old Mystic

evidence.claim: Route 27 follows the east bank of the Mystic River between Mystic and Old Mystic.
evidence.quote: The road along the east bank of the Mystic River, connecting the villages of Mystic and Old Mystic

evidence.claim: The state-designated scenic section runs from Jerry Browne Road in Stonington to Route 184 in Groton, closely paralleling the water and providing river views.
evidence.quote: Route 27 from the intersection of Jerry Browne Road (milepost 2.13) in Stonington to the Route 184 terminus (milepost 3.21) in Groton is a state designated scenic road. This portion of the route provides a view to the Mystic River, which it closely parallels.

evidence.claim: It forms the northern end of a highway that begins at US 1 in Mystic.
evidence.quote: Route 27 is a north–south state highway in southeastern Connecticut running for 3.21 miles (5.17 km) from U.S. Route 1 in Mystic (in the town of Stonington) to Route 184 in Old Mystic (in the town of Groton).

evidence.claim: The riverside road was Highway 344 in the 1920s, then became Route 169 in the 1932 renumbering.
evidence.quote: The road along the east bank of the Mystic River, connecting the villages of Mystic and Old Mystic, was a secondary state highway in the 1920s, with designation Highway 344. In the 1932 state highway renumbering, old Highway 344 was renumbered to Route 169.

evidence.claim: Route 27 began elsewhere in 1950, following the Colonel Ledyard Highway to Route 184.
evidence.quote: Route 27 was established in 1950, running from Route 12 in Ledyard to Route 184. The old Route 27 followed the path of the Colonel Ledyard Highway.

evidence.claim: The following year it absorbed the old Route 169 section through a short overlap with Route 184.
evidence.quote: By the following year, Route 27 was extended along old Route 169 via a short overlap with Route 184.

evidence.claim: In 1963, the portion north of Route 184 was removed, leaving the present route.
evidence.quote: the part of old Route 27 north of Route 184 was deleted in 1963, leading to its current configuration.

evidence.claim: Approaching the scenic section from Mystic, the road passes Mystic Seaport and crosses I-95.
evidence.quote: It passes by the Mystic Seaport and Old Mystic Village and then crosses I-95 at exit 101.

evidence.claim: North of the interstate it becomes Whitehall Avenue, then Main Street through Old Mystic.
evidence.quote: North of I-95 it becomes Whitehall Avenue then becomes Main Street as it runs through the village of Old Mystic

evidence.claim: From Jerry Browne Road, follow the river toward the village; the drive finishes a short distance beyond at Route 184.
evidence.quote: Route 27 ends a short distance later at an intersection with Route 184.

evidence.claim: The scenic section closely parallels the Mystic River, with views of the water.
evidence.quote: This portion of the route provides a view to the Mystic River, which it closely parallels.

evidence.claim: Much of the Mystic River is tidal: this is a 3.4-mile estuary fed chiefly by Whitford Brook and emptying into Fishers Island Sound.
evidence.quote: The Mystic River is a 3.4-mile-long (5.5 km) estuary in the southeast corner of the U.S. state of Connecticut.  Its main tributary is Whitford Brook. It empties into Fishers Island Sound

evidence.claim: It divides Mystic between Groton and Stonington.
evidence.quote: dividing the village of Mystic, Connecticut between the towns of Groton and Stonington.

evidence.claim: Three large shipbuilding firms operated along it in the nineteenth century; Mystic Seaport maritime museum now stands on the river.
evidence.quote: The Mystic River was the location of three large shipbuilding firms during the 19th-century, and it is now the home of the Mystic Seaport maritime museum.

evidence.claim: The Mystic River Historical Society traces the name to the Pequot missi-tuk, describing a large river driven into waves by tides or wind.
evidence.quote: The name Mystic is derived from the Pequot term "missi-tuk", describing a large river whose waters are driven into waves by tides or wind, according to the Mystic River Historical Society.

evidence.claim: Route 27’s scenic section follows the water closely enough to provide river views.

evidence.claim: At 39 Main Street, the former Mystic Bank presents three recessed arches beneath a pedimented gable.
evidence.quote: The Mystic Bank is a historic commercial building at 39 Main Street in the Old Mystic village of Stonington, Connecticut.

evidence.claim: Rectangular windows fill the outer bays, with the entrance between them.
evidence.quote: Each bay is set in a round-arch recess, with rectangular sash windows in the outer bays and the main entrance in the center bay.

evidence.claim: The bank was founded in 1833 to serve local shipbuilders and the surrounding rural communities.
evidence.quote: The Mystic Bank was founded in 1833 by a consortium of local businessmen as a service to the local shipbuilding community and the surrounding rural areas.

evidence.claim: It commissioned this brick building in 1856 as business expanded.
evidence.quote: The bank flourished, and was able to build this building in 1856 to accommodate its expanded business.
